# Label-Lattice Memoization — Stage A results (synthetic org, CPU only)

**Read this first.** Everything below comes from a *synthetic* organisation generated by `sim.py` under *assumed* parameters (listed below). No real ACL export, real read log, or real artifact workload was used. The numbers show how the idea behaves under these assumptions and where it breaks in a sweep; they are **not** evidence about any real company. The one hard methodological result is the *shape* of the sensitivity (what drives the falsifier), not the absolute percentages.

Source idea: `docs/long-context-research.md`, Idea 1, Stage A. Falsifier (from the report): *if ≥50% of read mass requires labels with ≤3 principals, drop the idea.* I evaluate it separately for raw-document reads (f) and derived-artifact reads (g); "PASS" = fraction < 50%, "FAIL" = ≥ 50%, "MIXED (k/5 pass)" = seeds disagree.

## Headline (baseline: medium structure, 5% private docs; 5 seeds, mean [min–max])

| | |
|---|---|
| Distinct entitlement signatures (10,000 users) | **9,859** [9,831–9,912]; 97.6% of users are alone in their signature |
| Distinct doc labels (200k docs) | **28,820** by ACL set / **27,941** by audience |
| Distinct derived-artifact labels (100k artifacts) | **55,345** symbolic / **19,028** by audience |
| Doc read mass servable from an item shared by ≥2 users (realized) | **92.9%** [88.0–95.3]; storage ratio per-user ÷ shared = **9.3×** |
| (f) Doc read mass needing a label with ≤3 principals | **8.5%** [6.0–13.7] → **PASS** (threshold 50%) |
| (g) Artifact read mass on labels with ≤3 principals | **40.8%** [33.6–49.6] → **PASS, but thin margin** (one seed at 49.6%) |

Key findings (all conditional on the assumed parameters):
1. **The "signatures ≪ users" hypothesis is refuted here.** Because each user carries a team + ~2.5 projects + ~1 cross-cutting group + a role, nearly every user has a unique group-set signature (9.9k of 10k; even 8.1k with *few large groups*). Sharing therefore cannot rely on users collapsing into a few signature classes. It works instead because **labels are per-document audiences, and many documents share a broad label** (200k docs → ~28k audiences; popular docs have large audiences).
2. **Raw-document sharing is robust; derived-artifact sharing is the fragile part.** The doc-level falsifier stays PASS up to ~40% private docs (all three structures; read mass ≈ private-doc fraction because popularity is type-neutral), is a coin flip at 50%, FAIL from 60%. Derived artifacts (label = intersection of 2–8 inputs' audiences) shrink the audience (median artifact-to-narrowest-input audience ratio 0.60 [0.50–0.86] over seeds; 56% of artifacts are strictly narrower than their narrowest input), so the artifact falsifier trips much earlier: PASS at ≤5% private for every structure, MIXED at 10–20%, FAIL at ≥30% (≥20% for many-small-groups).
3. **What kills it:** (i) a large share of read mass on per-user-private or ad-hoc-shared docs; (ii) many small project-level ACLs (many-small-groups structure) *combined with* intersections; (iii) private docs being read disproportionately (4× per-doc popularity at 20% private → doc-level 51.6%, MIXED). **What helps:** few large groups, broad/team/department ACLs, low ad-hoc sharing, private docs read less than shared ones. Worst-case combo (many small groups, 20% private, 50% small-group, 10% ad-hoc): docs 30.8% PASS but artifacts 65.5% FAIL. Best-case combo: 0.0% / 9.7%.
4. **Eager-on-write cost looks small *in this synthetic log*:** 191.6k of 200k docs get ≥1 read among 5M reads (Zipf 1.0), so eager and lazy computing are nearly the same count. That depends on read volume and popularity skew (not tested for much sparser logs).

Shared-store gain is real but modest in hit-rate terms: lazy per-user cache hit rate is already 64% (heavy re-reading, Zipf head), vs 96% for a shared lazy store (100% if eager). The bigger win is storage/compute: **9.3×** fewer entries for docs, **3.2×** for artifacts at baseline.

## Parameters (all assumed; see `sim.py` `Params`/`STRUCTURES`)

- Users 10,000; docs 200,000; doc reads 5,000,000; derived artifacts 100,000 (2–8 inputs, P(k=2..8) = .30/.25/.15/.10/.08/.07/.05; mean distinct inputs ≈ 3.1); artifact reads 1,000,000. Fixed seeds: run seed ∈ {1..5} with `SeedSequence([seed, 20261025])`; results fully deterministic (tested).
- Groups: company (everyone) → departments → teams (each team in one dept; membership of team implies its dept) ; projects (each has a parent team; user's project memberships: 1 + Poisson(λ), 65% from own team's projects, else global); cross-cutting groups (Poisson(λc) per user); one role per user. Popularity / size of groups ~ Zipf(exponent z), randomly permuted ranks.

| structure | depts | teams | projects | cross | roles | Zipf z | extra projects λ | cross λ | total groups | largest group |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| few_large | 8 | 40 | 80 | 20 | 10 | 0.8 | 1.0 | 0.5 | 159 (median size 183) | 3,064 users |
| **medium (baseline)** | 25 | 250 | 1,500 | 100 | 40 | 1.0 | 1.5 | 1.0 | 1,916 (median size 8) | ≈2.6k users |
| many_small | 60 | 1,000 | 6,000 | 400 | 100 | 1.0 | 2.0 | 1.5 | 7,561 (median size 2) | 2,079 users |

- Document ACL (= union of groups), by doc type: **private** (fraction p; ACL = one owner, owner chosen heavy-tailed lognormal σ=1); **ad-hoc** (3%: explicit list of 2–5 users); **small-group** (25%: 1 project, 30% a second); **broad** (the rest): company 10%, department 25% (20% a second), cross-cutting 15% (30% a second), role 5%, team 45% (25% a second).
- Doc popularity: Zipf exponent 1.0 over a random rank permutation, times `private_pop_mult` (1.0 = neutral, so read-mass share of private docs ≈ p). Reader of a doc = drawn from the doc's audience weighted by a lognormal(σ=1) user activity weight. So reads are always authorised and, structurally, "within the reader's groups".
- Derived artifacts (baseline `creator` mode): creator drawn ∝ their read count; inputs sampled from that creator's own read history (k of them). **Artifact label audience = bitset AND of the inputs' audiences** (a creator is always in it). Artifact popularity Zipf 1.0; readers drawn from the artifact's audience. Mode `random`: inputs are popularity-weighted random docs (not a worst case — it skews to hot, broad docs).
- Definitions: *entitlement signature* = hash of a user's effective group set. *Label* = for docs the ACL set (symbolic) and, canonically, the resulting audience set (two ACLs with the same audience count as one); *label audience size* = number of users who can read the item. Reads of an item "servable from a shared artifact" = realized: the item is read by ≥2 distinct users in the log (potential: audience ≥ 2). Per-user cache = unlimited-capacity cache keyed (user, item); shared store = keyed (item, label), computed once. Entries are unit size.
- Revocation unit tests (`test_revocation.py`, 9 tests, all pass) are described below.

## Where the idea survives / dies (summary of the sweep)

| Question | Answer under these assumptions |
|---|---|
| Doc-level falsifier (f) | PASS (all seeds) for private-doc share ≤ 40% in all three structures; MIXED at 50%; FAIL ≥ 60%. Crossing ≈ 50–54% mean. Structure matters little here (few_large 50.3%, medium 51.5%, many_small 53.8% at p=50%) because private docs dominate the ≤3 mass; structure matters at p=0 (2.7% / 3.5% / 7.2%). |
| Artifact falsifier (g) | PASS (all seeds) for p ≤ 5% in every structure; MIXED at 10–20% (few_large: PASS at 10%, MIXED at 20%; many_small: MIXED at 10%, FAIL at 20%); FAIL from p ≥ 30% (many_small ≥ 20%). Artifact audiences are ≈ half the size of the narrowest input. |
| Ad-hoc sharing | 15% ad-hoc docs (vs 3%) pushes the baseline artifact falsifier to FAIL (54.0%). |
| Small-group (project) ACL share | Raises artifact ≤3 mass (25.6% at 0% → 47.1% at 50% small-group docs), barely moves doc-level. |
| Private-doc popularity | Decisive: with `private_pop_mult=4`, 20% private docs already give 51.6% (doc) / 75.5% (artifact); with 0.25, 50% private docs give 23.6% (doc). The sweep "private fraction" is really about private *read mass*. |
| Signature count | ~8k–10k of 10k in all scenarios: group-set signatures don't compress users in this synthetic org. (Not tested: orgs where almost all users have only team+role.) |

## Revocation test (report's second-pass reviewer note)

Implemented in `lattice.py` (reference model: ACL service with monotonically increasing epoch; artifact store keyed (id, version), label = list of input ACLs, tombstones, entitlement leases) and `test_revocation.py` (run `python3 test_revocation.py`; **9/9 pass**):
- write restricted doc → derive artifact from restricted + broad doc → authorised user reads it; users in only one input's audience are refused (label = intersection, not union);
- revoke a user's group membership → with push invalidation the user is refused immediately (lag 0) and dependants are tombstoned until re-derived (version 2); other users are served again after re-derivation;
- push disabled/delayed (worst case): cached decision may be served only within the lease window; refusal occurs no later than `revoke_time + lease` for several revocation offsets (lease = 30 s simulated); a very long lease (1000 s) *does* keep serving a revoked user until delivery/expiry — that is the documented risk of long leases;
- ACL tightening tombstones exactly the dependent artifacts, not unrelated ones; declassification is re-derivation from the broadly visible subset with separate lineage (the restricted summary is never relabelled);
- epoch monotonic. Two extra tests check the simulator itself: determinism, and that a sampled artifact's audience size equals the naive set intersection.
This tests the *logic* of the revocation design in a toy model; it says nothing about real distributed lag, caches, or covert channels (timing, size, existence oracles were not modelled).

## Caveats (honest limits)

- Synthetic org; every number depends on the assumed memberships, ACL mix, popularity and reader model. Real orgs have correlated memberships (people on the same team share projects), inherited folder ACLs, link-sharing, group nesting and churn that this model only crudely mimics; direction of the bias is unknown.
- Reader choice is doc-first (document drawn by popularity, reader drawn from its audience), not a behavioural model of users; reads of a user are authorised by construction. Popularity is independent of audience size except via `private_pop_mult`.
- Derived-artifact workload (2–8 inputs from a creator's reads, 1M reads) is a guess; no real agent trace. The `random` mode is not adversarial.
- Hit-rate/storage use unit-size items, unlimited caches, no versions/updates/churn; "shared" assumes perfect dedup by (item, label). KV-block size, position-independence quality (Stage B) and eager-compute cost in tokens are not measured.
- Label canonicalisation by audience is favourable (it merges ACLs with identical audiences); symbolic counts are also reported. Empty-audience docs (≈0.2%) get zero popularity.
- ACL hierarchy is shallow (company ⊃ dept ⊃ team; projects flat); no deny rules, no group-membership churn over time, no per-chunk ACLs.
- Seeds vary notably at the Zipf head (e.g. doc ≤3 mass 6.0–13.7% at baseline); 5 seeds is a minimum, ranges are shown.
- Not measured: entitlement-signature classes as the "principal" unit for the ≤3 test (I use users), so audiences are measured in users.

## What real ACL exports are needed

Permissions only (no content): for a Google Drive / Workspace, GitHub org, or similar — per-file/repo ACL entries (group/user/link/domain-wide), group membership lists with nesting, owner ids, folder inheritance, and file creation/modification and (if available) access/audit logs for the read distribution. From that I could compute the same (a)–(g) directly: real signature counts, real label audience sizes, and share of read (or file) mass with audience ≤3 — plus how much real "private" and "ad-hoc shared" content exists, which this sweep shows is the decisive quantity. Derived-artifact labels would still need an assumed or traced agent workload (which documents get combined).

## Files

- `sim.py` — simulator + metrics (`python3 sim.py` runs one baseline seed to /tmp/ll_one.json; `--quick` for a small one)
- `run_all.py` — all scenarios × 5 seeds (`NPROC=3 python3 run_all.py`; ~7 min on 3 cores, ~450 MB per worker); per-run raw JSON in `runs/`
- `results.json` — aggregated results (per-scenario params, mean/min/max, per-seed rows, audience histograms, verdicts)
- `make_report.py`, `tables.md` — table generation
- `lattice.py`, `test_revocation.py` — reference model and tests
- `RESULTS.md` — this file
